extracted.intended_audience: students and readers interested in comics theory / visual arts learners
extracted.subtask_description: A short analytical summary of Chapters 7–9 of Scott McCloud's Understanding Comics, extracting conceptual and practical principles about creating and reading comics (stages of creation, color theory, and communication). Intended as a study/essay resource for visual-arts students.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Six Steps (idea, form, idiom, structure, craft, surface)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The six steps refer to the stages of the creation of any artwork, which include idea, form, idiom, structure, craft, and surface (170)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the six-step sequence as a framework for creating or analyzing comics: begin with purpose (idea) and move toward execution (surface). Note McCloud's warning that, despite the logical order, many artists learn these steps from the end to the beginning because early stages seem simpler. Treat each stage as interconnected and expect unique problems at each point; decisions made at one stage affect solutions and the final style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and functions of art
rubrics_metrics.description: McCloud defines art as any activity which does not take place due to the basic instincts of humanity such as "survival and reproduction" (164).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or creating comics, consider art's broader functions: exercise for the mind, a way to lash out or express emotion to calm down, and a pastime leading to discoveries. Recognize that 'elements of art' may appear across occupations and that 'pure art' (created without mercenary purpose) is an ideal—this frames intent and value judgments about work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color: commerce and technology considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Color's role in comics is influenced by two factors: commerce and technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan color choices with practical constraints in mind: printing technologies, production costs, and commercial expectations affect what colors are feasible and how they will be used. Understand basic technical concepts (e.g., additive primaries) to anticipate how colors reproduce and interact in the medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color as an expressive tool (mood, symbol, contrast, depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Color is used as a tool helping to express the characters’ emotions; complementary colors were used to create contrast; colors of costumes turned into symbols representing characters; color helps express moods, highlight key elements, and create depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color deliberately to convey emotion, emphasize narrative elements, and build spatial depth. Consider symbolic associations (costume hues becoming character shorthand) and employ complementary or subtle palettes depending on whether you want bold contrast or nuanced atmosphere. Track trends (e.g., shift from stark complementary colors to subtler hues) when choosing a stylistic approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing color versus black-and-white (impact on focus and idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: McCloud states black and white comics "do not shift the focus of the reader’s attention to the surface of the image due to the absence of color," while bright colors make pictures look more realistic and detailed and can be used to create entire worlds; black-and-white can present simple but thought-provoking ideas more effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select color or black-and-white based on desired reader focus and the message: use color to increase realism, detail, worldbuilding, and emotional signaling; use black-and-white to avoid surface distractions and foreground concept, tone, or idea. Match medium to communicative goals rather than defaulting to color for its visual appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of representation and the communication problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of a future picture appears in the artist's mind, but imagination is more powerful than technical skill, making it almost impossible to express an idea in all its beauty. Enhancing skills increases the percentage of the initial idea that is visually represented, but full understanding is regarded as an unachievable goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating comics, acknowledge and plan for inevitable loss between conception and representation. Aim to maximize fidelity through skill and craft while accepting that some aspects of an idea will be transformed. Use composition, sequencing, and visual shorthand to convey as much intent as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-creator partnership in meaning-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers and creators will always be partners in the art process; the primary goal of this collaboration is establishing a steady contact helping the idea to change its physical form with the imperceptible loss of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comics with the reader's role in mind: anticipate interpretation, provide cues that guide but do not fully determine meaning, and craft sequences that invite the reader to complete or co-create narrative sense. Test readability and interpretive affordances to reduce miscommunication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic decision-making defines final style
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-making skills of an artist define his or her final style; each stage in the process is interconnected with unique problems, and solutions shape style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat stylistic choices as outcomes of repeated decisions across idea, form, idiom, structure, craft, and surface. Evaluate how problem-solving at each step (e.g., how to render a face, pace a sequence, or choose a palette) accumulates into recognizable style; deliberate decisions yield consistent stylistic identity.
